analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to disclose how fast executive pay and worker pay are rising, side by side.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor in the House before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal securities law so that public companies (except young 'emerging growth' firms) must report, in their annual filings, the percentage raise executives got in the last fiscal year, the percentage raise all other employees got, the ratio between those two numbers, and how each compares to inflation. The idea is to make pay-raise gaps between the corner office and the rest of the workforce visible to investors, employees, and the public every year. The bill died in committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of large public companies, who would get an annual, standardized snapshot of whether executives' raises are outpacing everyone else's; investors and proxy advisors who use pay data; and unions, advocacy groups, and reporters who could cite the numbers in wage negotiations and coverage. There is already a 'pay versus performance' rule requiring some executive pay disclosure, but this bill adds the year-over-year raise comparison between executives and non-executive employees.

how_it_helps.text: Public companies must disclose the percentage increase in the median annual total compensation of executive officers over the last completed fiscal year [S3].
They must also disclose the percentage increase in median pay for all employees excluding executives, plus the ratio between the executive raise and the worker raise [S3].
Both the executive raise and the worker raise must be compared to the change in the Consumer Price Index, so readers can see whether pay is keeping up with inflation [S3].
The disclosures go into the company's annual report filed with the SEC, creating a standardized, yearly, public record [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies would bear the cost of calculating and verifying the new disclosures each year. Executives and companies whose raises dramatically outpace worker raises would bear a reputational cost, since the ratio would be published annually. No taxpayer funds are involved; this is a disclosure requirement on private filings.

drawbacks.text: The requirement is disclosure only: companies could still grant any raises they wanted, and the bill includes no penalty, cap, or bargaining right tied to the numbers [S3].
Compliance costs fall on issuers, who would need to calculate median pay for all employees each fiscal year — an administrative burden that falls hardest on mid-sized public companies [S3].

Median raise percentages can be distorted by workforce changes (hiring, layoffs, shifts in job mix), so the disclosed ratios could mislead more than inform in some years — an objection securities-law practitioners commonly raise to pay-disclosure metrics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but limited: annual, standardized visibility into whether executive raises are outpacing worker raises and inflation, usable by employees, investors, and reporters. The cost is modest compliance work for issuers. The honest limitation is that transparency is not enforcement — the bill changes what companies must say, not what they may pay. On balance it is a low-cost, low-coercion accountability tool rather than a fix for pay inequality.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, it never got a cosponsor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on September 14, 2023 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action appears in the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public companies and their executives, who avoid a mandatory annual side-by-side comparison of executive and worker raises and any reputational fallout it might produce.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured; it was a single-sponsor bill that died in committee.

industries.note: They would face new annual disclosure costs and, more significantly, public scrutiny of the ratio between executive raises and worker raises each year. Industry groups generally resist expanded pay-disclosure mandates on those grounds.
Standardized raise-ratio data would give them another input for voting on executive compensation and engaging with companies. The public gets the same data for free.
